title: Biogeochemical Cycles: Carbon, Nitrogen and Phosphorus
seo_title: Year 11 Earth and Environmental Science: Biogeochemical Cycles Worksheets
standard_code: Earth and Environmental Science Unit 2: Energy for biogeochemical processes
standard_text: The carbon cycle: reservoirs, fluxes and residence times; photosynthesis, respiration and combustion; the nitrogen cycle (fixation, nitrification, denitrification); the phosphorus cycle; human effects on cycles, including fossil fuels, fertilisers and eutrophication. (Senior Secondary Earth and Environmental Science, Unit 2: Earth processes – energy transfers and transformations)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Earth and Environmental Science worksheets on biogeochemical cycles: carbon reservoirs and fluxes, the Keeling curve, the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, eutrophication and blue carbon. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Matter cycles; energy from the Sun drives the cycles.
key_sub: Nitrogen: fixation → nitrification → uptake → decomposition → denitrification.
body_html:
How to think about it

Carbon moves between the atmosphere, biosphere, oceans and rocks. Photosynthesis removes CO₂; respiration, decomposition and combustion return it. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon stored for millions of years, so atmospheric CO₂ rises.

Nitrogen gas must be fixed by bacteria (such as Rhizobium in legume roots), lightning or industry before plants can use it; nitrifying bacteria make nitrates and denitrifying bacteria return N₂ to the air. Phosphorus has no gas phase: it comes from weathered rock. Too much nitrogen and phosphorus in waterways causes eutrophication.

Example

A store gains 120 and loses 115 units per year. Net change?

120 − 115

Answer: +5 units per year (it grows)

Example

CO₂ rose from 340 ppm in 1980 to 420 ppm in 2024. Mean rate?

80 ppm ÷ 44 years

Answer: about 1.8 ppm per year

Common mistakes

  • Saying plants take nitrogen gas straight from the air.
  • Forgetting that the oceans and rocks are carbon stores.
  • Thinking phosphorus cycles through the atmosphere.

faq.q: Why does atmospheric CO₂ go up and down each year on the Keeling curve?
faq.a: Northern Hemisphere forests take in CO₂ in their spring and summer and release it in autumn and winter; most land plants are in the north.

faq.q: What causes blue-green algal blooms in Australian rivers?
faq.a: Warm, slow water with too many nutrients (phosphate and nitrate from fertiliser and sewage) lets cyanobacteria grow fast, using up oxygen and making toxins.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from the geosphere into the atmosphere?
c: shells and sediment settling on the seafloor and becoming rock
rock weathering that uses CO₂ from rainwater
CO₂ dissolving into the ocean surface
items.e: Match the process to the flow.

items.q: Which way does rock weathering that uses CO₂ from rainwater move carbon?
c: from the atmosphere into the geosphere
from the biosphere into the geosphere
from the geosphere into the atmosphere
from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere
items.e: Follow the carbon from one sphere to another.

items.q: Which part of a living thing needs phosphorus?
c: DNA, ATP and phospholipids in membranes
items.e: Bones and teeth also contain calcium phosphate.

items.q: How does deforestation affect the carbon cycle?
c: it reduces photosynthesis and releases stored carbon when trees burn or decay
items.e: Land clearing is a source of CO₂.

c: it removes CO₂ from the air
it adds a potent greenhouse gas to the atmosphere, which later breaks down to CO₂
items.e: Methane traps far more heat than CO₂ per molecule.

items.q: What is the source of energy for nutrient cycling in ecosystems?
items.e: Energy flows, nutrients cycle.

items.e: Plants and algae fix carbon.

items.q: How are carbonate rocks such as limestone part of the carbon cycle?
c: marine organisms build shells from dissolved carbonate; these become rock that stores carbon for millions of years
they are part of the water cycle only
items.e: Weathering and volcanoes slowly return it.

items.e: Termites also help in many Australian ecosystems.

items.q: What is the role of decomposers in nutrient cycles?
c: they add nitrogen gas to the air directly
they break down dead matter, releasing nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus back to the soil
items.e: Without them nutrients would stay locked in dead matter.

c: dead organisms are buried and slowly changed by heat and pressure over millions of years
items.e: Coal comes from swamp plants; oil and gas mostly from marine plankton.

items.q: The secondary consumers contain 24000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the tertiary consumers contain 1920 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 8.00%.

items.q: How does fertiliser runoff threaten the Great Barrier Reef?
c: it makes the water too cold
nutrients feed algae and the larvae of crown-of-thorns starfish, which eat coral
items.e: Reducing runoff is part of reef management.

items.q: What is primary productivity?
c: the rate at which producers make biomass by photosynthesis
items.e: GPP − respiration = NPP.

items.q: The producers contain 20000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the primary consumers contain 1600 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 8.00%.

items.q: Why is phosphate needed by plants?
c: to make ATP, DNA and phospholipids
items.e: Phosphate comes from rocks, not the air.

items.q: The primary consumers contain 10000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the secondary consumers contain 1200 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 12.0%.

items.q: What is eutrophication?
c: excess nutrients cause algal growth, leading to low oxygen levels in water
items.e: Bacteria decomposing dead algae use up oxygen.

items.q: The secondary consumers contain 20000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the tertiary consumers contain 1000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 5.00%.

items.q: What is nitrification?
c: bacteria convert ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates
items.e: Nitrates are taken up by plant roots.

items.q: What is leaching?
c: nitrates are washed out of soil into rivers and lakes
items.e: It can cause eutrophication.

items.q: Which ocean habitats along Australian coasts store large amounts of 'blue carbon'?
items.e: Their muddy sediments lock up carbon.

items.q: Why is nitrogen gas (N₂) not directly useful to most plants?
c: it is too rare in the air
the triple bond is very strong, so it must first be fixed into ammonia or nitrate
items.e: Air is 78% nitrogen.

items.q: How is the phosphorus cycle different from the carbon and nitrogen cycles?
c: it happens only in the air
it has no significant gas phase in the atmosphere; phosphorus comes from weathering rocks
items.e: Phosphate moves through soil, water and organisms.

items.q: What is the main way carbon enters ocean food webs?
c: volcanoes on the sea floor only
items.e: Phytoplankton do about half of Earth's photosynthesis.

items.q: What is nitrogen fixation?
c: breaking down proteins into amino acids
converting nitrogen gas into ammonia or nitrogen compounds that plants can use
items.e: Done by bacteria, lightning and the Haber process.

items.q: The secondary consumers contain 12000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the tertiary consumers contain 1440 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 12.0%.

items.q: What is nitrogen fixation?
c: bacteria such as Rhizobium convert nitrogen gas into ammonia
items.e: Rhizobium lives in root nodules of legumes.

items.q: Why do fires in Australian bushland release nutrients?
c: burning turns plant material into ash rich in phosphorus and other minerals
fire adds nitrogen gas to soil
items.e: Some nitrogen is lost to the air as gases.

items.q: What do saprobionts do in the nitrogen cycle?
c: decompose dead organisms, releasing ammonium ions (ammonification)
items.e: They secrete enzymes and absorb the products.
